meta.subtitle: Nuclear-anchored power generator selling into data-center demand, now digesting the $21.8 billion Calpine acquisition

analystCommentary: We rate Constellation Energy (CEG) HOLD with a $270-$330 target range against a $263.46 price as of September 22, 2026. The company calls itself the largest nuclear energy company in the U.S., and since the January 2026 Calpine acquisition it also runs a large gas fleet and retail platform. FY25 revenue, before Calpine, rose {+ +8.3% +} to $25.5B; with Calpine included, second-quarter 2026 revenue rose {+ +23.0% +} year over year to $7.5B. Profit fell in that quarter but rose over the six months, and we set out both readings in Financials. The case rests on per-share earnings rather than revenue. Consensus EPS of $12.13 for FY26E and $13.25 for FY27E supports a Base case of $300, but our Bear case, in which EPS stays near the trailing level and the multiple compresses, sits at $185. Weighted, the scenarios give a fair value of $293.75 and expected upside of +11.5%, yet bear-case downside of -29.8% leaves reward/risk at 0.39x, short of the BUY threshold. Our earlier report on this filing rated the shares BUY; the change comes from pricing the Bear case on its own earnings story, and the Valuation section shows how close the call is.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Constellation Energy Corporation is a competitive power producer and retail electricity supplier headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland. Its 10-Q for the period ended June 30, 2026 describes a fleet of 55 gigawatts across nuclear, natural gas, oil, geothermal, hydro, wind and solar facilities, which the company says can power the equivalent of 27 million homes and provides about 10% of the nation's clean energy. The company also calls itself a leading competitive retail supplier serving approximately 2.5 million customer accounts, including 80% of the Fortune 100. On January 7, 2026 it acquired Calpine Corporation for a purchase price of approximately $21.8 billion, paid with 50 million newly issued shares and approximately $4.5 billion in cash on hand. After divestitures tied to regulatory approvals, Calpine brings approximately 23 GWs of predominantly natural gas, geothermal, battery storage and solar capacity, plus a retail platform serving approximately 62 TWhs of load annually. Two sources disagree on the company's shape. The vendor's company description cites approximately 31,676 megawatts of capacity and five segments (Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, New York, ERCOT and Other Power Regions); we use the 10-Q figure, the company's own count for the enlarged fleet. The pack shows revenue only as one consolidated total, $25.5B in FY25, with no split by those segments, so we quote no regional mix.

thesis.body: Constellation pairs a large nuclear fleet with a growing book of long-term contracts sold into data-center and corporate demand, and Calpine adds dispatchable gas capacity and retail scale. The shares trade far below the 52-week high of $412.70 and nearer the low, while consensus still expects EPS to rise through FY27E; no source in our pack explains the decline. If that consensus is met, our Base case has upside. The difficulty is the downside. Earnings follow power and fuel prices, as the 10-K warns, Calpine carries integration and dilution risk, and second-quarter 2026 margins were thin, although the six-month and trailing figures read stronger (see Financials). On our scenarios the reward does not yet pay for that risk, and our target range sits below the Street's $348.55 consensus target.

catalysts: Completion of the LS Power divestitures that satisfy the remaining Calpine regulatory commitments, which the company expects by the end of 2026.
Further data-center and long-term nuclear contracts, building on the CyrusOne agreements at the Freestone Energy Center and the new nuclear PPAs (see Growth).
The 2029/2030 PJM Base Residual Auction, which runs under the same FERC-accepted price collar as the 2028/2029 auction that cleared at the cap.
Earnings contribution in coming quarters from capacity that entered service in 2026, including the Pin Oak Creek Energy Center and the Pastoria Power Bank.
Second-half 2026 results that show whether operating margin recovers from its second-quarter level as Calpine is integrated.
risks: Power and fuel price exposure; see Risks.
Calpine integration costs and liabilities; see Risks.
PJM and FERC market-design changes; see Risks.
Russian nuclear fuel sanctions and supplier performance; see Risks.

financials.incomeCommentary: FY25 revenue was $25.5B, up {+ +8.3% +} year over year, after {+ +24.4% +} in FY22, {+ +2.0% +} in FY23 and {- -5.4% -} in FY24. The series is uneven, and the captured excerpts do not explain the swings, so we do not assign a cause. Profit has moved more than revenue. Operating margin rose from -1.8% in FY21 to 18.5% in FY24, then fell to 12.1% in FY25 as EBITDA declined to $5.7B from $7.1B; FY25 net income was $2.3B and diluted EPS fell to $7.40 from $11.89. In the second quarter of 2026, which includes Calpine while the year-ago quarter does not, revenue rose {+ +23.0% +} year over year to $7.5B, but operating margin was 7.7%, below the FY25 level. GAAP net income attributable to common shareholders was $513 million in the quarter versus $839 million a year earlier, a {- -$326 million -} change. The six-month figures point the other way: the same measure was $2,103 million versus $957 million, {+ +$1,146 million +}, and the trailing twelve-month operating margin of 14.7% sits above FY25's. Trailing net margin was 11.1%. The captured MD&A ends before management's discussion of these results, so we assign no cause to the weak quarter or the strong half. In the second quarter, revenue grew while profit fell; whether that quarter or the half-year is the better guide to the rest of 2026 is the main open question for the earnings path, and it is the question our Bear and Base cases split on.
financials.balanceCommentary: At FY25 year-end, before the Calpine close, the company carried $9.0B of total debt against $3.6B of cash and short-term investments, for net debt of $5.4B, the same as in FY24. Total equity was $14.9B and the current ratio was 1.53. Those year-end figures put net debt below one year of EBITDA. The trailing net debt to EBITDA of 2.9x is much higher, so leverage has risen since year-end. The pack does not show the June 30, 2026 debt balance, and we do not tie the rise to a specific item, though it follows the cash portion of the Calpine payment. Trailing interest coverage of 5.9x and a trailing current ratio of 1.46 leave room to carry that debt. The pending sales to LS Power, five PJM gas plants with approximately 4.4 GWs valued at $5.0 billion and the 606 MW Brazos Valley Energy Center at $860 million, both before closing adjustments, are expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. The company presents them as satisfying regulatory commitments and does not say in the captured excerpt how it will use the proceeds; if retained, they would offset part of the cash spent on Calpine.
financials.cashflowCommentary: FY25 operating cash flow was $4.2B, positive after four years of outflows that reached $5.3B in FY23; the captured excerpts do not explain the earlier outflows. Capital expenditure was $2.9B, leaving free cash flow of $1.3B and a 5.0% FCF margin; FY25 is the one positive year in the five-year series. That free cash flow covered dividends of $0.5B and repurchases of $0.4B, the latter down from $1.0B in each of FY23 and FY24, with a small remainder. The trailing FCF yield is 0.3%, so over the latest twelve months the business generated little free cash relative to its market value. One positive year after four negative ones is not yet a pattern, and capital expenditure already absorbs most of operating cash flow, which leaves little internal funding for growth projects without new debt or asset sales.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On the company column, CEG trades at 25.7x trailing earnings, 3.0x sales and 14.2x trailing EV/EBITDA. The vendor labels its 21.7x forward P/E as next-twelve-month, but that multiple lines up with the price over FY26E EPS of $12.13, so we read it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $13.25 the multiple is about 19.9x. The step down from trailing to forward multiples depends on consensus EPS growth arriving, and the quarterly record so far is mixed (see Financials). We value the shares on earnings rather than sales because consensus EPS is the quantity our scenarios price. The Street is constructive: 22 analysts rate the stock Buy 19, Hold 3, Sell 0, with a consensus target of $348.55 (+32.3%), a median of $350.50 and a range of $290.00 to $441.00. The pack carries no peer multiples, so we anchor on the company's own multiples and consensus EPS rather than on a peer premium or discount.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Data-center demand turns into more long-term contracts on top of the new nuclear PPAs and the Freestone agreements, and Calpine integrates without the EPS dilution the 10-K flags as possible. FY27E EPS of $13.25 is met, and the shares earn a P/E above today's 25.7x trailing multiple as the market also prices capacity value beyond FY27E, such as a 2029/2030 PJM auction at the cap. The price sits between the Street median of $350.50 and the high of $441.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The LS Power divestitures close and Calpine integration proceeds without a further margin setback. Consensus FY26E revenue and the FY27E EPS consensus are broadly met, despite the second-quarter shortfall against the full-year revenue pace (see Growth), and the shares hold a P/E slightly above the 21.7x current-year multiple on that FY27E EPS.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Power prices soften and Calpine proves costly and dilutive, as the 10-K warns it may. Full-year EPS stays near the trailing twelve-month level implied by the trailing P/E, short of the FY26E consensus of $12.13, and with growth stalled the P/E compresses into the high teens, below the 19.9x the shares carry on FY27E EPS. A 2029/2030 PJM auction near the $175/MW-day floor would also weigh on value beyond FY27E.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight Base at 50% and Bull and Bear at 25% each. The weighted values are $97.50, $150.00 and $46.25, for a probability-weighted fair value of $293.75, expected upside of +11.5%, bear-case downside of -29.8% and reward/risk of 0.39x. Expected upside clears the BUY line, but reward/risk does not, so the label derives HOLD. The Bear case is a real downside: at $185 it sits below the 52-week low of $228.63, and the past year's range shows the shares can move that far. Its weight rests on its own story. The second-quarter fall in net income and margin shows earnings can fall short of the consensus path, which argues against a lower weight; the six-month rise in net income argues against a higher one. The deciding split is close, and we say so: moving five points of weight from Bear to Bull would derive BUY. The case for that move is the lengthening contracted book and the stronger six-month and trailing profit figures. The case against is that the latest quarter went the wrong way and no source explains it. We do not think either side outweighs the other yet, so we hold Bull and Bear level and accept the HOLD the arithmetic derives. The target range of $270 to $330 brackets both the Base case and the weighted fair value.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Revenue is shown as one consolidated total with no split by the regions the vendor lists, so this entry covers the whole company. Operationally the fleet reaches several markets named in the 10-Q, including PJM, where the company is selling five gas plants to LS Power. In Texas the company has the Freestone Energy Center and the Pin Oak Creek Energy Center, which serves the ERCOT grid, and is selling the Brazos Valley Energy Center in ERCOT. In California the Pastoria Solar Project is contracted by the California Department of Water Resources, and the co-located Pastoria Power Bank carries a 15-year power purchase agreement with Pacific Gas and Electric Company. Because the pack carries no segment revenue, we do not quote a regional or fuel-type mix.

moatFactors.name: Licensed nuclear fleet
moatFactors.body: The licensed nuclear fleet delivers around-the-clock output that intermittent resources cannot. New nuclear capacity faces licensing, siting and capital barriers, which protects the incumbent. The protection cuts both ways: the 10-K lists the renewal of operating licenses among its regulatory risks, so the barrier that keeps rivals out must also be renewed.

moatFactors.name: Long-term contracted demand
moatFactors.body: The new nuclear PPAs run 15 to 20 years with investment-grade customers, and the CyrusOne and Pastoria agreements add contracted demand (see Growth). Contracts of this length convert merchant output into predictable revenue. The limit is timing: the nuclear PPAs begin only in 2029 through 2032, so they do not yet shield current earnings.

moatFactors.name: Retail scale
moatFactors.body: With Calpine's platform added, the company describes itself as the nation's leading competitive retail electric supplier. The 10-K notes that wholesale generators, including the company, use their retail operations to hedge generation output, which supports this factor. The same 10-K warns that barriers to entry in retail can be low and that retail competition depends on continued support of the host state.

moatFactors.name: Merchant price exposure
moatFactors.body: The 10-K says the company is exposed to commodity price risk for fuel and for the unhedged portion of its generation portfolio, so earnings and cash flows move with spot and forward market prices (see Risks). The pack does not show how much output is hedged or contracted. That exposure limits durable pricing power, and it is the main reason we rate the moat narrow rather than wide.

businessMoat.durability: The durable core is the licensed nuclear fleet, and demand for firm, clean power supports its value. Two things keep the moat narrow. First, the unhedged portion of the portfolio stays exposed to market prices, and the new long-term nuclear PPAs do not start until 2029 through 2032; the pack does not show the share already contracted. Second, the value of the fleet depends on market rules that the 10-K says can change with little notice, such as the PJM price collar and FERC's co-location orders. The contracted book is the mechanism that could widen the moat as those contracts start. Until then we judge the moat narrow and improving.

points: Consensus FY26E revenue of $35.1B, a {+ +38% +} step-up over FY25, reflects the enlarged company. Second-quarter revenue growth of +23.0% ran below that pace, and the pack does not show first-quarter revenue, so we cannot say how much of the gap the rest of the year must close; this shortfall is the counter-case to the Base case's revenue assumption.

Data-center demand is being contracted directly. In first-quarter 2026 the company signed a 380 MW agreement with CyrusOne to serve a new data center next to the Freestone Energy Center, plus an exclusive agreement for a 380 MW Phase 2; these add to the 400 MW Calpine-CyrusOne agreements at the Thad Hill Energy Center announced in the second half of 2025.

The company signed an additional 920 MW of long-term nuclear PPAs of 15 to 20 years with investment-grade customers, beginning 2029 through 2032; the 176 MW Walmart agreement among them will enable a 30 MW capacity expansion at the Dresden Clean Energy Center.

New capacity is reaching service: the 460 MW Pin Oak Creek Energy Center, a gas peaking plant, achieved commercial operation in April 2026, the 105 MW Pastoria Solar Project was commissioned that month, and the 80 MW/320 MWh Pastoria Power Bank came online in July 2026.

In July 2026 the entire RTO cleared PJM's 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction at the $325/MW-day price cap, including all submitted CEG units. That supports capacity revenue for the 2028/2029 delivery year, after the FY27E horizon our scenarios price, so it bears on value beyond FY27E rather than on near-term earnings.

This growth costs capital and arrives late. Capital expenditure already absorbs most of operating cash flow (see Financials), the new nuclear PPAs start in 2029 or later, and the LS Power sales will remove part of the acquired fleet.

management.leadership: This section rests on the proxy statement filed March 19, 2026. Its ownership table lists five named executive officers by surname but gives no titles, so we assign none. The CEO's compensation is developed and administered by the Compensation Committee and approved by the independent members of the Board. In its Compensation Discussion and Analysis, management states that total shareholder return since the company became independent in 2022 has significantly outperformed the S&P 500 and its peer group; we attribute that claim to management and do not verify it. The test for leadership now is the Calpine integration and the margin trend that follows it (see Financials).
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation has shifted from buybacks to scale. Repurchases fell in FY25 (see Financials), and the Calpine purchase, paid partly in new shares, enlarged the share count. The 10-K filed February 24, 2026 warns that the acquisition brings reduced ownership and voting power for current shareholders, potential dilution to earnings per share, and no assurance of the dividends at the current rate post-acquisition. With a 0.65% dividend yield, the dividend is a small part of the return case. The larger question is whether the deal earns its cost in per-share earnings, which the Valuation section tests against consensus.
management.governance: The proxy statement filed March 19, 2026 says the Board has affirmatively determined that none of the non-employee directors who served in 2025, nor any nominee, has a material relationship with the company, and that each non-employee director is independent under the Corporate Governance Principles. All members of the Audit & Risk Committee and the Compensation Committee are independent under Nasdaq and SEC standards. The proxy lists pay practices that include awarding the majority of NEO pay as variable cash and equity, capped incentive awards, clawback provisions, double-trigger change-in-control vesting, no employment agreements with the CEO or NEOs, no hedging or pledging of company stock by NEOs or directors, and no option repricing without stockholder approval. It reports no related person transactions identified in 2025. For outside holders this is a clean profile that lowers agency risk, though it does not by itself make a large acquisition a good use of capital.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider ownership is small. The proxy shows directors and executive officers as a group of 21 individuals holding 1,140,643 shares as of March 2, 2026, which it states is less than 1% of shares outstanding; the individual holdings are led by a non-employee director, Lawless, with 161,967 shares and a named executive officer, Dominguez, with 157,074. The proxy's list of holders above 5% mixes filing dates. The Vanguard Group (11.7%) and BlackRock (7.2%) are shown as of December 29, 2023 per Schedule 13G/A filings, while ECP ControlCo, LLC (7.0%) is shown as of January 14, 2026 per a Schedule 13G. State Street (5.7%) and Capital International Investors (5.5%) are also listed; their footnotes are not in the captured excerpt. No holder approaches control, and alignment rests more on the stock-ownership requirements the proxy describes than on insider stakes.

idiosyncratic: Calpine integration: the 10-K filed February 24, 2026 warns of a complex, costly and time-consuming integration with potential unknown liabilities and the possible loss of key employees and customers, as well as legal and regulatory risks and valuation risk that could negatively impact future operating results.

Power and fuel prices: the 10-K states that earnings and cash flows are exposed to spot and forward market prices and to the cost and availability of nuclear fuel, natural gas and oil. In some hours supply can exceed demand, producing negative prices and lost revenue for baseload plants such as nuclear, and hedges can prove ineffective.

Market design: PJM capacity revenue runs under a collar of approximately $175/MW day to $325/MW day that FERC accepted for the 2028/2029 and 2029/2030 auctions, and depends on FERC's co-location and large-load orders. The 10-K warns that price caps and policies favoring new resources could lead to the premature retirement of existing resources.

Nuclear fuel: the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act bans Russian low-enriched uranium absent a DOE waiver, and in November 2024 the Russian government imposed temporary restrictions on enriched-uranium exports to the U.S. The company relies on long-term contracts with diverse suppliers and has contracted to increase its fuel inventory, but supplier non-performance could have a material adverse impact.

State policy: the Illinois Climate and Equitable Jobs Act requires certain gas units to eliminate CO2 emissions by January 1, 2030, subject to reliability exceptions (PJM found the Zion Energy Center needed for reliability), and California's Cap-and-Invest Program, extended through January 1, 2046, requires covered plants to surrender compliance instruments.
risks.systemic: The 10-K lists access to capital markets among its market and financial risks, and the company has just paid for part of a large acquisition in cash, so higher interest rates or tighter credit would weigh on it. Power demand depends on economic activity and on the pace of data-center buildout. The 10-K also notes that the market price of power is affected by the price of the marginal fuel, in particular natural gas, so lower gas prices would reduce what unhedged nuclear output earns. Finally, the shares carry an earnings multiple that assumes growth (see Valuation), and that multiple would compress if sentiment around data-center power demand cooled.

body: We rate Constellation Energy HOLD with a target range of $270 to $330 against a $263.46 price. The Base case has upside if consensus EPS growth arrives, and the contracted book is lengthening, but our Bear case leaves reward/risk below the BUY threshold. This replaces the BUY in our earlier report on this filing; the change comes from pricing the Bear case on its own earnings story rather than from any change in the price.

The rating is HOLD rather than SELL because consensus still expects EPS growth and the six-month and trailing profit figures are stronger than the second quarter alone. It is not a BUY because second-quarter margins were thin and quarterly net income fell year over year (see Financials), and because the Calpine integration carries risks the company itself flags.

On these scenarios the label is sensitive to price. A fall of a few percent from the current price would derive BUY, with reward/risk the test that flips first; a rise to somewhat above our $300 Base case would derive SELL. On the fundamentals, we would move to BUY if second-half 2026 results follow the six-month earnings trend rather than the second quarter's, which would justify less weight on the Bear case, and we would reconsider toward SELL if operating margin stays near its second-quarter level, which would put the FY26E consensus out of reach.
